articles.heading: General Regulations for Competitions
articles.content: All FIDE-rated competitions must be conducted in accordance with the FIDE General Regulations for Competitions. Organisers must submit an application to FIDE or the relevant continental federation in advance. The application must include the proposed regulations, time control, number of rounds, prize fund, and the name of the Chief Arbiter. FIDE approval is required for events to be rated.

articles.heading: Announcements and Invitations
articles.content: A tournament must be announced publicly at least 30 days before the start for national events and at least 60 days for international events. The announcement must include: dates, venue, time control, number of rounds, entry fee, prize fund, pairing system, and the name of the Chief Arbiter. Any changes to announced conditions must be communicated promptly to all registered participants.

articles.heading: Withdrawals and Forfeits
articles.content: A player who withdraws from a tournament after it has started must notify the arbiter immediately. Results already scored against a withdrawing player are cancelled if the player has completed less than 50% of their games. If 50% or more of games are completed, all results stand. A player who fails to appear for a game without informing the arbiter loses the game by forfeit.

articles.heading: Restricted Drawing of Lots
articles.content: When drawing of lots is required to determine pairings, colour assignments, or seedings, FIDE recommends a restricted drawing process. This ensures that players from the same federation or club are not paired against each other in the first round when possible. The arbiter supervises the drawing of lots and documents the results.

articles.heading: Tie-Break Regulations — General
articles.content: When players finish a tournament with equal scores, tie-break criteria are used to determine final standings. The tie-break system to be used must be announced before the start of the tournament. FIDE recommends a hierarchy of tie-break systems. Common tie-break methods include: direct encounter, Buchholz system, Sonneborn-Berger, number of wins, and progressive score.

articles.heading: Buchholz System
articles.content: The Buchholz score is the sum of the scores of all of a player's opponents. Median Buchholz cuts the highest and lowest opponent scores. Truncated Buchholz (BH-C1) removes only the lowest opponent score. The Buchholz system is the most widely used tie-break in Swiss tournaments. A higher Buchholz score means a player faced stronger opponents, indicating a better performance.

articles.heading: Sonneborn-Berger System
articles.content: The Sonneborn-Berger score is used primarily in round robin tournaments. It is calculated as the sum of the scores of opponents beaten plus half the sum of the scores of opponents drawn with. Opponents who are lost to are not counted. This system rewards winning against stronger opponents more than winning against weaker opponents.

articles.heading: Play-Off and Tie-Break Regulations
articles.content: For determining a single champion or qualifying spots, play-off games may be used. The standard FIDE play-off sequence is: rapid game(s), then blitz game(s), then an Armageddon game if still tied. In an Armageddon game, White has more time but must win; a draw counts as a win for Black. The time controls for each play-off stage are specified in the tournament regulations.
